The minimum number of triangular edges and a symmetrization
for multiple graphs
Zolt´an F¨uredi ∗
Zeinab Maleki †
This work was done while the authors visited the Department of Mathematics and
Computer Science, Emory University, Atlanta, GA, USA.
Abstract
We give an asymptotic formula for the minimum number of edges contained on triangles in a graph
having n vertices and e edges. Our main tool is a generalization of Zykov’s symmetrization what we
can apply for several graphs simultaneously.

Graphs with few triangular edges
Erd˝os, Faudree, and Rousseau [2] showed that a graph on n vertices and at least ⌊n2/4⌋+1 edges has at least
2⌊n/2⌋+ 1 edges on triangles. To see that this result is sharp, just consider the graph obtained by adding
one edge to the side of the complete bipartite graph K⌈n/2⌉,⌊n/2⌋with ⌈n/2⌉vertices. More generally,
for a graph G let E(G, K3) denote the set of edges of G contained on triangles, Tr(G) := |E(G, K3)|,
Tr(n, e) := min{Tr(G) : |V (G)| = n, e(G) = e}. With this notation the above result of Erd˝os, Faudree,
and Rousseau can be reformulated as
Tr(n, ⌊n2/4⌋+ 1) = 2⌊n/2⌋+ 1.

Let \(s(G)\) be the number of non-triangular edges in \(G\), and let \(s(n,e)\) be the maximum of \(s(G)\) over \(n\)-vertex graphs with at least \(e\) edges. Füredi and Maleki [4] made the following conjecture.

**Conjecture 1** (Füredi and Maleki [4]). *For every \(n\) and \(e\), there is a graph \(H = G(a,b,c)\) with \(n\) vertices and at least \(e\) edges such that \(s(H) = s(n,e)\).*

<visual_element id="e1">
Figure 1 graph \(G(a,b,c)\): a left clique labeled \(A\), a top-right independent set labeled \(C\), and a bottom independent set labeled \(B\), with many edges from \(B\) to \(A \cup C\) and no edges between \(A\) and \(C\).
</visual_element>

**FIGURE 1.** The graph \(G(a,b,c)\)

Note that the aforementioned result of Erdős, Faudree and Rousseau [3] confirms Conjecture 1 for \(e = \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + 1\), (consider the graph \(G(2,\lfloor n/2 \rfloor,\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 2)\)). Füredi and Maleki proved an approximate version of their conjecture.

**Theorem 2** (Füredi and Maleki [4]). *For every \(n\) and \(e\) there is a graph \(H = G(a,b,c)\) such that \(|H| = n\), \(e(H) \ge e\) and \(s(H) \ge s(n,e) - 3n/2\).*

We prove the conjecture exactly, for large \(n\).

**Theorem 3.** *There is \(n_0\) such that for every \(n \ge n_0\) and every \(e\), there is a graph \(H = G(a,b,c)\) such that \(|H| = n\), \(e(H) \ge e\) and \(s(H) = s(n,e)\).*

The proof for \(e\) that is close to either \(n^2/4\) or \(\binom{n}{2}\) is easier; we discuss it briefly in the next section. The middle range, when \(e\) is bounded away from both \(n^2/4\) and \(\binom{n}{2}\), is the heart of the proof, and we elaborate more about it in Section 3.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Given integers a,b,c, let G\left(a,b,c\right) denote the graph on n=a+b+c vertices, which consists of a clique A of size a and two independent sets B and C of sizes b and c, respectively, such that all edges between B and A\cup C induces a complete bipartite graph {K}_{b,a+c}. In other words, the graph G\left(a,b,c\right) can be obtained from {K}_{b,a+c}, by embedding a clique of order a into the part of size a+c. Note that G\left(a,b,c\right) has \left(\genfrac{}{}{0ex}{}{a}{2}\right)+\left(a+c\right)b edges, and it has \left(\genfrac{}{}{0ex}{}{a}{2}\right)+ab=m-bc triangular edges. In 2017, Füredi and Maleki [18] conjectured that the minimizers of the number of triangular edges are graphs of the form G\left(a,b,c\right) or subgraphs of such graphs.

Conjecture 1.2. ((Füredi–Maleki, 2017))Let m>{n}^{2}/4 and G be an n-vertex graph with m edges that minimizes the number of triangular edges. Then G is isomorphic to a subgraph of G\left(a,b,c\right) for some a,b,c.

Particularly, Füredi and Maleki [18] proposed a numerical conjecture, which states that every n-vertex graph with m edges has at least g\left(n,m\right) triangular edges, where

g\left(n,m\right)=\mathrm{min}\left\{m-bc:a+b+c=n,\left(\genfrac{}{}{0ex}{}{a}{2}\right)+b\left(a+c\right)\ge m\right\}.

We remark that Conjecture 1.2 characterizes the structures of the minimizers, while the latter conjecture gives a lower bound only. By using a generalization of Zykov's symmetrization method, Füredi and Maleki [18] showed a lower bound: if G is a graph on n vertices with m>{n}^{2}/4 edges, then G has at least g\left(n,m\right)-3n/2 triangular edges. Soon after, Gruslys and Letzter [19] proved an exact version of the result of Füredi and Maleki. Let \mathbf{NT}\left(G\right) be the set of non-triangular edges of G. The following result was established in Ref. [19].

Theorem 1.3. ((Gruslys–Letzter, 2018))There is {n}_{0} such that for any graph G on n\ge {n}_{0} vertices, there exists a graph H=G\left(a,b,c\right) on n vertices such that e\left(H\right)\ge e\left(G\right) and \mid \mathbf{NT}\left(H\right)\mid \ge \mid \mathbf{NT}\left(G\right)\mid .

Theorem 1.3 shows that for sufficiently large n, the minimum number of triangular edges among all n-vertex graphs with at least m edges is achieved by the graph G\left(a,b,c\right) or its subgraph for some a,b,c. We refer the readers to Ref. [19] for more details and Ref. [20] for the study on the minimum number of edges that occur in odd cycles.

Here we focus on the notion of tight cycles. An \(r\)-uniform *tight cycle* is a sequence \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) of at least \(r+1\) distinct vertices satisfying that \(v_i,\ldots,v_{i+r-1}\) is an edge for every \(i \in [k]\) (indices are added modulo \(r\)). Denote by \(f_r(n)\) the maximum possible number of edges in an \(r\)-graph on \(n\) vertices that contains no tight cycles. So we will be interested in estimating \(f_r(n)\) for \(r \ge 3\).

Consider the \(r\)-graph on vertex set \([n]\) whose edges are \(r\)-subsets of \([n]\) that contain 1. This hypergraph has \(\binom{n-1}{r-1}\) edges and contains no tight cycles (indeed, it is easy to see that the edges of any tight cycle cannot be covered by a single vertex). In particular, \(f_r(n) \ge \binom{n-1}{r-1}\). Sós and, independently, Verstraëte (see [4, 6]) conjectured that this bound is tight for large enough \(n\). This was refuted by Huang and Ma [2], who showed that, for \(r \ge 3\), there exists \(c=c(r)>1\) such that \(f_r(n) \ge c \cdot \binom{n-1}{r-1}\) for large \(n\). A clever construction due to B. Janzer [3] implies the best known lower bound to date, namely that \(f_r(n) \ge \Omega(n^{r-1}\log n/\log\log n)\) for \(r \ge 3\).

Notice that \(f_r(n) \le \binom{n}{r}\), trivially. An old paper of Erdős [1] implies the following improvement of this trivial bound: \(f_r(n)=O(n^{r-2^{-(r-1)}})\). For \(r=3\), this was improved by Verstraëte (unpublished) who showed \(f_3(n)=O(n^{5/2})\). Recently, these bounds were significantly improved by Sudakov and Tomon [5], who proved that \(f_r(n) \le n^{r-1}e^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}\) for \(r \ge 3\), establishing that \(f_r(n)=n^{r-1+o(1)}\). Our contribution is to sharpen the error term \(e^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}\) in Sudakov and Tomon’s bound, as follows.

**Theorem 1.** *Let \(r \ge 3\). Then \(f_r(n)=O(n^{r-1}(\log n)^5)\).*--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
